nodes.label: ADR 1 — Build a failover lib
nodes.rationale: Platforms depend on many referential systems whose unavailability makes the platform unusable, and the impact compounds with each dependency. Since referential data changes rarely and business often accepts slightly stale data, keep a local store written on every successful call, recover from it on failure, and bound staleness with a business-agreed expiry plus cleanup. Must stay very simple because it will be adopted by many services.

nodes.label: ADR 2 — Dedicated @Failover annotation
nodes.rationale: Reusing @FeignClient was possible, but a dedicated @Failover annotation reads better at the call site and gives a natural home for the unique name and expiry configuration. Trade-off accepted: it only works through Spring AOP.

nodes.label: ADR 3 — Referential metadata: asOf / upToDate
nodes.rationale: Callers need to know how old recovered data is (asOf) and whether it is live or recovered (upToDate). Delivered as a deliberately tiny domain module (one annotation, one interface, one abstract class); both contracts are optional — no contract applied means no metadata populated.

nodes.label: ADR 4 — RecoveredPayloadHandler SPI
nodes.rationale: Gives consumers a hook to decide what a null/absent recovery means (e.g. return an empty collection instead of null) rather than baking one policy into the handler.

nodes.label: ADR 5 — FailoverStore abstraction and built-in stores
nodes.rationale: Ship basic storage options rather than force every consumer to write one: INMEMORY (ConcurrentHashMap, explicitly not for production), CAFFEINE, JDBC (needs JdbcTemplate + ObjectMapper) and CUSTOM. store and delete may run asynchronously because store I/O otherwise taxes the caller's latency.

nodes.label: ADR 6 — FailoverExecution SPI (BASIC vs RESILIENCE)
nodes.rationale: Two execution strategies behind one SPI: BASIC try/catch for the zero-dependency case and RESILIENCE for Resilience4j circuit-breaker wrapping, selected by failover.type.

nodes.label: ADR 7 — Scheduled expiry cleanup
nodes.rationale: Expired entries must be reclaimed or the store grows without bound; ExpiryCleanupScheduler runs the delete on a cron rather than on the hot path.

nodes.label: ADR 8 — FailoverReporter monitoring
nodes.rationale: Reporting split behind publishers (logger, Micrometer) so observability backends are pluggable; later renamed to the observer/publisher stack by ADR 29.

nodes.label: ADR 9 — KeyGenerator SPI
nodes.rationale: The store key is derived from method arguments by default, with a named-bean override so consumers can key on something other than the raw argument list.

nodes.label: ADR 10 — DefaultFailoverStore defensive copy
nodes.rationale: Callers mutate the recovered ReferentialPayload (upToDate, asOf), so the store clones on the way out; without the copy the in-memory store would hand out its own live entry and be corrupted by the caller.

nodes.label: ADR 11 — Store wrapping via BeanPostProcessor (Deprecated)
nodes.rationale: Originally wrapped raw FailoverStore beans with DefaultFailoverStore → FailoverStoreAsync via static @Bean BeanPostProcessors. Deprecated once multi-tenancy exposed two fatal flaws (see ADR 16): a BPP only sees Spring-managed beans, and @Async only works through a Spring AOP proxy.

nodes.label: ADR 12 — MethodExceptionPolicy (RETHROW / NEVER_THROW / CUSTOM)
nodes.rationale: What to do when recovery cannot produce a value is a business decision, not a library one — so it is an enum-selected pluggable strategy rather than a hardcoded rethrow.

nodes.label: ADR 13 — JDBC native merge/upsert with dialect detection
nodes.rationale: Dialect-specific single-statement upsert avoids the insert-then-update race and round trip, with an ANSI insert/update fallback for unrecognised databases so no dialect is unsupported.

nodes.label: ADR 14 — DatabaseResolver SPI
nodes.rationale: Database-product detection is isolated behind a strategy interface so dialect selection is testable and overridable rather than being inline metadata sniffing.

nodes.label: ADR 15 — FailoverStoreQueryResolver co-locates JDBC query building
nodes.rationale: All SQL construction (table prefix, dialect merge, column resolution) lives in one single-responsibility collaborator so FailoverStoreJdbc holds execution only.

nodes.label: ADR 16 — Remove BeanPostProcessor store wrapping (supersedes ADR 11)
nodes.rationale: A BPP only intercepts Spring-managed beans, so per-tenant stores built inside a TenantStoreFactory would silently skip async/defensive-copy wrapping; and @Async on a factory-created instance degrades to synchronous with no error. Wrapping is therefore assembled explicitly at one visible point, and @EnableAsync is removed from the autoconfigure module as the correct responsibility boundary.

nodes.label: ADR 17 — TenantStoreFactory SPI
nodes.rationale: Separates per-tenant store creation from store assembly so the assembler does not need to know how a tenant's backend is constructed.

nodes.label: ADR 18 — FailoverStoreAutoConfiguration as central assembler
nodes.rationale: One auto-configuration class owns the whole store chain so the wrapping order is explicit, deterministic and reviewable in a single place instead of emerging from bean-post-processing order.

nodes.label: ADR 19 — FailoverStoreAsync holds an explicit TaskExecutor
nodes.rationale: @Async silently degrades to synchronous when the instance is not a Spring proxy; an injected TaskExecutor works regardless of how the store was constructed and makes the concurrency strategy testable.

nodes.label: ADR 20 — MultiTenantFailoverStore as routing decorator
nodes.rationale: Tenant routing must sit outside the per-tenant wrapping so every tenant's store receives the identical DefaultFailoverStore/async chain; placement relative to the async decorator determines whether the tenant context is resolved on the caller thread.

nodes.label: ADR 21 — Multi-tenant auto-configuration and TenantResolver SPI
nodes.rationale: Multi-tenancy is a separate opt-in auto-configuration so the single-tenant path carries none of its conditionals; how the current tenant is discovered is a TenantResolver SPI because it is application-specific.

nodes.label: ADR 22 — FailoverKeyGenerator UUID key normalisation
nodes.rationale: Argument-derived keys are unbounded in length and overflow the VARCHAR(256) key column; hashing to a fixed-width MD5/UUID makes every key storable regardless of argument size.

nodes.label: ADR 23 — PayloadSplitter scatter/gather storage
nodes.rationale: Batch-fetch methods keyed on the whole argument suffer subset and superset misses ('1,2,3' misses an entry stored as '1,2,3,4'), so the cache is only useful when callers repeat the exact same id set. Splitting the composite payload into per-entity slices keyed through the same FailoverKeyGenerator chain makes partial recovery possible; opt-in via @Failover(payloadSplitter=...) so the default single-key path is unchanged.

nodes.label: ADR 24 — Parallel scatter/gather via CompletableFuture + injected Executor
nodes.rationale: Sequential dispatch costs the sum of slice latencies (10 slices × 50ms = 500ms). Explicitly rejected ForkJoinPool/parallelStream: slices are I/O-bound and the common pool risks starvation. A SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor with virtual threads avoids platform-pool exhaustion; a null executor keeps the sequential default.

nodes.label: ADR 25 — ContextPropagator SPI for parallel scatter
nodes.rationale: Dispatching slices onto executor threads loses thread-local context (tenant, tracing, MDC); the SPI captures on the caller thread and restores on the worker, with a composite for combining propagators.

nodes.label: ADR 26 — Instant instead of LocalDateTime for expiry
nodes.rationale: LocalDateTime carries no zone, so expiry computed on one node and evaluated on another in a different timezone is ambiguous; Instant removes the ambiguity for multi-node/multi-timezone deployments.

nodes.label: ADR 27 — Migrate deprecated JdbcTemplate overloads
nodes.rationale: Varargs overloads replace the deprecated Object[] + int[] forms, which also removes the java.sql.Types coupling.

nodes.label: ADR 28 — domain attribute for shared store partitioning
nodes.rationale: A scatter/gather batch endpoint and a single-entity endpoint fetch the same entities but would otherwise write to different partitions; a shared domain lets them share store entries. Mismatched expiry inside one domain is warned at startup.

nodes.label: ADR 29 — Observer/Publisher SPI and MDC logger refactor
nodes.rationale: Renames the reporter stack to observer, publishes through an ObservablePublisher SPI with a composite, and makes logging MDC-safe so observability never leaks context across threads.

nodes.label: ADR 30 — SpringContextFailoverScanner replaces Reflections scanning
nodes.rationale: Enumerating Spring beans finds exactly the @Failover methods that are actually advisable, removing the package-to-scan configuration burden and the Reflections/Guava dependency.

nodes.label: ADR 31 — failover-observable-micrometer as an optional module
nodes.rationale: Micrometer meters and the Actuator health indicator are extracted into an opt-in module so core carries no Micrometer dependency.

nodes.label: ADR 32 — PayloadSplitterExecutionException wrapping
nodes.rationale: A failure inside consumer-written splitter code is otherwise an opaque stack trace; wrapping every call with splitter name and operation context makes the diagnosis obvious.

nodes.label: ADR 33 — doRecoverAll iterates all slices
nodes.rationale: Slice count is user-controlled through splitOnRecover rather than inferred by the framework, so doRecoverAll simply iterates whatever the splitter returns.

nodes.label: ADR 34 — ScatterGatherFailoverHandler.recoverAll() throws
nodes.rationale: Inheriting the default recoverAll in scatter mode would silently execute the wrong path; an explicit UnsupportedOperationException fails loudly instead.

nodes.label: ADR 35 — Empty splitOnRecover returns null, not merge([])
nodes.rationale: Merging an empty list would fabricate an empty successful result indistinguishable from a real one; returning null keeps 'nothing recovered' honest.

nodes.label: ADR 36 — splitOnRecover single-placeholder contract
nodes.rationale: When delegating to DefaultFailoverHandler.recoverAll the splitter must return exactly one placeholder context, making the delegation contract explicit rather than implied.

nodes.label: ADR 37 — Payload deserialization allowlist
nodes.rationale: JsonSerializer.toClass loading an arbitrary class name from a store row is a deserialization-gadget surface; restricting it to an allowlist auto-derived from discovered @Failover payload packages is secure by default with no consumer configuration.

nodes.label: ADR 38 — Scatter/gather per-slice timeout
nodes.rationale: A hung slice would block the caller through allOf().join(); failover.scatter.timeout bounds the join — a timed-out recover slice counts as not recovered, a timed-out store slice surfaces.

nodes.label: ADR 39 — Error propagates unwrapped; never recover on a failing JVM
nodes.rationale: Treating an OutOfMemoryError as an upstream failure would run recovery logic on a dying JVM; the aspect rethrows Error unwrapped instead.

nodes.label: ADR 40 — Multi-tenant strict mode
nodes.rationale: Without strict mode an unconfigured tenant silently falls through to the global table, cross-contaminating data; the flag rejects (or WARNs once on) tenants absent from the map.

nodes.label: ADR 41 — failover.store.async.failed metric
nodes.rationale: The async store is a silently-degrading layer — an executor-side write failure never reaches the caller — so it must publish its own failure counter to be visible at all.

nodes.label: ADR 42 — FailoverScanner moved to a neutral core package
nodes.rationale: The scanner stopped being an observability-only concern once store deserialization safety consumed it, so core.observable.scanner → core.scanner reflects the shared ownership.

nodes.label: ADR 43 — Dialect integration tests via Testcontainers
nodes.rationale: Dialect-specific merge SQL cannot be validated against H2; real PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB containers exercise it, profile-gated (dialect-its) and excluded from the default build because they need Docker. Oracle stays string-asserted for lack of a freely-pullable image.

nodes.label: ADR 44 — Concurrency tests for tenant routing and the async store
nodes.rationale: computeIfAbsent must yield exactly one store per tenant under contention, and the async executor path must not lose writes — both are only provable with contention tests, kept in the default build.

nodes.label: ADR 45 — ArchUnit architecture tests
nodes.rationale: Encodes invariants a reviewer would otherwise have to remember: no ThreadLocal inside the async decorator, *Store naming, acyclic slices, and split-package guards.

nodes.label: ADR 46 — PIT mutation testing with a 95% gate
nodes.rationale: Line coverage does not prove the expiry and key boundary logic is actually asserted; a mandated 95% mutation gate (currently 96%, test strength 99%) does, profile-gated so the default build stays fast.

nodes.label: ADR 47 — JDBC insert→update race: bounded retry over silent drop
nodes.rationale: When a concurrent expiry delete removes the row between a failed INSERT and the follow-up UPDATE, the write vanished silently. One bounded re-INSERT (2 attempts max) fixes the common case; losing every attempt is abandoned at warn because the data is a regenerable cache. Native-merge dialects were never affected.

nodes.label: ADR 48 — INFO lifecycle event, DEBUG payload body
nodes.rationale: Serialising the full ReferentialPayload for an INFO log put payload serialisation on the hot path; only the name stays at INFO, the body moves to DEBUG.

nodes.label: ADR 49 — Extract scatter/gather collaborators
nodes.rationale: ScatterGatherFailoverHandler became a thin facade over PayloadScatter / PayloadGather / SliceDispatcher / SplitterInvoker; public API and behaviour unchanged, construction moved to a builder instead of overloaded constructors.

nodes.label: ADR 50 — Metrics helper: concatenation over String.format
nodes.rationale: Metric-key construction sat on the recover path; replacing String.format with concatenation plus typed collect overloads made the recover-bag build ~3.6× faster (JMH 744 → 204 ns/op).

nodes.label: ADR 51 — Per-method failover outcome metric
nodes.rationale: failover.recovery.outcome.total{name,domain,method,outcome} gives failover / recovery / non-recovery rates per intercepted method, recorded once per call and tagged by the actual SimpleClass#method.

nodes.label: ADR 52 — Method-aware FailoverHandler contract + AbstractFailoverHandler
nodes.rationale: Threading the intercepted Method through store/recover/recoverAll replaces ADR 51's ad-hoc mechanism; AbstractFailoverHandler bridges method-agnostic handlers so only custom SPI implementations migrate. Accepted as a breaking SPI change because it is the honest contract.

nodes.label: ADR 53 — Cross-module JaCoCo coverage gate
nodes.rationale: Per-module coverage hides gaps at module boundaries; failover-test-report unpacks all classes, merges every exec file and fails verify below 95% line / 95% branch repo-wide.

nodes.label: ADR 54 — Collapse four property-gated store beans into one
nodes.rationale: Four @ConditionalOnProperty variants for the async × multitenant matrix duplicated assembly logic; a single failoverStore bean builds the chain imperatively and makes per-tenant-async explicit. Refines ADR 18, behaviour unchanged.

nodes.label: ADR 55 — Embedded Failover Dashboard
nodes.rationale: Operators could only read failover config from source and KPIs from a Prometheus/Grafana stack. A springdoc-style batteries-included panel closes that gap, but an on-by-default operational UI is a security hazard — hence a separate starter, enabled=false by default, no new instrumentation (KPIs derived from existing counters), a vendored CDN-free Chart.js, a fail-closed access gate, and allow-insecure refused outright under the prod profile. History is a process-local ring, deliberately not a TSDB.

nodes.label: ADR 56 — Payload-at-rest encryption for the JDBC store
nodes.rationale: PayloadCipher SPI plus EncryptingSerializer over the JDBC store using an ENC(<cipherId>:…) envelope so ciphertext is self-describing and rotation is a write-switch only; opt-in, and the b64 default is explicitly marked non-secure so nobody mistakes it for encryption.

nodes.label: ADR 57 — Async executor back-pressure
nodes.rationale: Unbounded virtual-thread dispatch has no admission control; BoundedTaskExecutor adds a semaphore guard that keeps tasks on virtual threads (no thread-pool swap), with concurrency-limit plus a rejection-policy (DISCARD default). Unbounded remains the default so existing behaviour is unchanged until configured.

nodes.label: ADR 58 — Non-durable store in production: advisory WARN over fail-fast
nodes.rationale: Profile-aware fail-fast was rejected as brittle (profiles are not a reliable production signal); instead the WARN names jdbc as the recommended production store and points at store decision/topology docs.

nodes.label: ADR 59 — Count async submit-time rejection
nodes.rationale: Executor rejection at submit time (ABORT policy or shutdown) was a saturation blind spot; it now emits the existing failover.store.async.failed meter rather than adding a new meter or tag.

nodes.label: ADR 60 — Allowlist strict mode: fail-closed on an empty allowlist
nodes.rationale: ADR 37 left one fail-open edge: an empty resolved allowlist disabled the restriction entirely, so a misconfiguration (scanner found nothing, AOP not wired) silently reopened the gadget surface. strict-allowlist makes empty mean deny-all; introduced false in 2.x and flipped to true in 3.0.0 because a major version is the point to stop shipping the fail-open default. The normal scanner-derived path is unchanged in either mode.

nodes.label: ADR 61 — Built-in AES-GCM payload cipher
nodes.rationale: ADR 56 shipped the SPI but only a non-secure b64 default, so real encryption required consumer crypto code. AesGcmPayloadCipher (id aesgcm) auto-registers from failover.store.jdbc.encryption.key to give usable encryption-at-rest out of the box.

nodes.label: ADR 62 — Opt-in JDBC live-entries gauge
nodes.rationale: Capacity visibility needs a row count, but a COUNT(*) per scrape is a real tax on a large table — so FailoverStoreJdbc implements FailoverStoreSizeAware and the gauge is off by default behind live-entries-gauge-enabled.

nodes.label: ADR 63 — Startup warning for un-advisable @Failover placement
nodes.rationale: An @Failover on an interface, a non-public/static/final method or a final class is never advised and fails silently at runtime; the scanner WARNs at startup instead, and self-invocation is documented.

nodes.label: ADR 64 — Startup warning for recoverAll without a payloadSplitter
nodes.rationale: recoverAll=true with no payloadSplitter silently falls back to single-key recover, so the feature appears configured but does nothing; the scanner WARNs at startup.

nodes.label: ADR 65 — Event-driven snapshot publishing with throttle and backoff
nodes.rationale: Fixed-interval polling pushed snapshots even when no metric events occurred, and mixed HTTP transport with publish orchestration in the wrong module. Replaced by metric-event-driven pushes throttled to one per interval-seconds via AtomicLong CAS, with WARN-once backoff; SnapshotPushClient abstracts transport so failover-observable-micrometer stays free of spring-web, and BoundedTaskExecutor(limit=1, DISCARD) means a second push while one is in flight is dropped because the in-flight push already carries the latest snapshot.

nodes.label: ADR 66 — Decoupled heartbeat liveness tracking
nodes.rationale: Inferring liveness from snapshot freshness conflated 'alive' with 'has recent metric events' (a quiet healthy instance read as DOWN) and used a kilobytes-of-JSON payload as a liveness signal. A separate {"instanceId"} heartbeat drives LiveStatus LIVE/DOWN/UNKNOWN while DOWN instances keep contributing last-known metrics. Polling is correct here — unlike snapshots, heartbeats must fire even with no metric events. Opt-in on both sides, default off.

nodes.label: ADR 67 — Reset-aware aggregate and bounded instance retirement
nodes.rationale: Peer snapshots carry cumulative counters that reset on restart, so the instant aggregate dropped while the trend graph stayed smooth — two views of the same data disagreeing. SnapshotBaseline folds pre-restart totals into a per-instance carry-forward (detected by a drop in cumulative total). Separately, naive eviction would violate the invariant that a dead peer's counts keep contributing, so unseen instances retire into retiredAggregate() and compact into a bounded tombstone past 100 entries — heap stays bounded under pod churn and cluster totals never shrink.

nodes.label: ADR 68 — Rolling-window dashboard health classification
nodes.rationale: Lifetime-cumulative counters meant an endpoint degraded correctly but never recovered — errors from hours ago kept it DEGRADED after 10,000 clean calls. RollingHealthWindow reconstructs a last-N-calls window by diffing cumulative totals per poll, needing no new instrumentation; deliberately not reusing FailoverApiHealthTracker (different module, hardcoded window, gauge-internals read path). Trade-off: ordering within one poll interval is not preserved. Scoped to the local source; prometheus/shared-store aggregate differently.

nodes.label: ADR 69 — Specific authorization-denial messages for the dashboard gate
nodes.rationale: Spring's default 403 is blank, so an operator who logs in via OIDC but has no GrantedAuthoritiesMapper cannot tell that mapping is the missing piece. DashboardAccessDeniedHandler names the missing role/authority in the body (generic text for EXPRESSION, whose sub-clause failure cannot be introspected) and logs the principal's actual authorities server-side only. Accepted trade-off: the required role string is disclosed, but only to already-authenticated callers.

nodes.label: ADR 70 — No auto-DDL and a durable heartbeat store for the JDBC tier
nodes.rationale: Four issues at once: (1) a library must not issue CREATE/ALTER against a consumer's database, so auto-DDL is removed outright with no flag, matching failover-store-jdbc which never auto-created FAILOVER_STORE; (2) SharedStore/Jdbc records lacked @ConstructorBinding, so Spring's binder treated the two-constructor record as ambiguous and silently ignored YAML; (3) the process-local HeartbeatStoreInmemory left every peer UNKNOWN when the dashboard is embedded in multiple instances sharing one database, hence HeartbeatStoreJdbc; (4) @ConditionalOnBean across independently-conditioned auto-configurations in different modules is unreliable without an explicit ordering edge — proven with an ApplicationContextRunner in both declaration orders — fixed with @AutoConfiguration(afterName=...). Timestamps moved to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE with per-dialect precision caps.
